questions.title: Sets practice 1
questions.explanation: The `&` operator computes intersection, keeping only values present in both sets. The result remains a set, not a list.

questions.title: Sets practice 2
questions.prompt: Which expression finds courses completed by Ada but not Ben?
choices: ada - ben
ada | ben
ada & ben
ben - ada
questions.explanation: Set difference keeps members from the left set that are absent from the right. Here the result is `{"MATH120"}`.

questions.title: Trace Sets
questions.code:
courses = ["CS101", "MATH120", "CS101", "ENG101"]
unique_courses = set(courses)
print(len(unique_courses))
print("CS101" in unique_courses)
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
questions.explanation: Repeated values disappear when the list becomes a set. The result has three unique course codes even though the source list has four items. The resulting output is '3\nTrue'.

questions.title: Sets practice 5
questions.prompt: How does `clubs.discard("Chess")` behave when "Chess" is not in the set?
choices: It does nothing and leaves the set unchanged
It raises a KeyError
It adds "Chess" to the set
It empties the set
questions.explanation: `discard` removes the value if present and simply does nothing if it is absent, so the set is untouched. `remove` is the version that raises a KeyError on a missing value. `discard` never adds anything or clears the set.

questions.title: Empty set syntax
questions.prompt: Which empty collection does `{}` create in Python?
choices: An empty dictionary, not an empty set.
An empty set with no values yet.
An empty tuple with no positions.
An empty list that removes duplicates automatically.
questions.explanation: `{}` is reserved for an empty dictionary. To make an empty set, use `set()`. Non-empty set literals such as `{1, 2, 3}` look similar to dictionary braces, so the empty case is the one students usually have to memorize.

questions.title: Ignoring duplicates
questions.prompt: A club sign-in sheet only needs each student name once. Which collection matches that rule?
choices: A list, because duplicate names should be kept exactly as entered.
A set, because duplicate names have no extra meaning.
A tuple, because the sign-in list should never change.
A dictionary with every name stored as the same value.
questions.explanation: Sets keep membership, not repeated copies. Adding the same name twice still leaves one name in the set. That is perfect for questions like "who attended at least once?" but not for questions that need counts or order.

questions.title: Set order
questions.prompt: Why should code avoid asking for "the first item" in a set?
choices: Sets can only store numbers, so text has no position.
Sets keep every duplicate, so first depends on count.
Sets do not promise a meaningful item order.
Sets cannot be looped over at all.
questions.explanation: A set is about membership. You can loop through it, but the order is not the point and should not control program logic. If position matters, use a list; if uniqueness matters, use a set.

questions.title: Removing optional values
questions.prompt: A program should remove `"Chess"` from a set if it is present, but do nothing if it is absent. Which method fits?
choices: Use `remove`, because it ignores missing values.
Use indexing, because sets support numeric positions.
Use `clear`, because it removes only one chosen value.
Use `discard`, because missing values are allowed.
questions.explanation: `discard` removes the value when it exists and does not raise an error when it is missing. `remove` is stricter and raises a KeyError for a missing value. Choose based on whether missing data is normal or a bug.

questions.title: Comparing groups
questions.prompt: Two study groups need to find topics they both selected. Which set operation expresses that overlap?
choices: Intersection with `&`, because it keeps values found in both sets.
Union with `|`, because it keeps only values that match.
Difference with `-`, because it combines both groups.
Indexing with `[0]`, because the first shared value is enough.
questions.explanation: Intersection keeps only the items that appear in both sets. Union keeps everything from either set, and difference removes one group's items from another. Naming the relationship first makes the operator easier to choose.

questions.title: Starting an empty set
questions.prompt: A loop will collect unique parking zones as it scans tickets. How should the empty collection start?
choices: Use `{}` and add zones later.
Use `set()` and add zones later.
Use `()` and assign into indexes later.
Use `[]` because lists automatically remove duplicates.
questions.explanation: Start with `set()` when the goal is unique membership. `{}` would create a dictionary, and a list would keep duplicates unless extra checks are added. The empty-start syntax matters because the later `.add(...)` calls depend on having a real set.
